meetings.title: Annual Town Meeting
meetings.date: Monday, May 4, 2026 · 7:00 PM · ABRHS Auditorium, 36 Charter Road
meetings.sessionNote: Night 1 of 2 · 40 articles on the warrant

articles.title: Appropriations for Municipal Operating Budget
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will raise and appropriate, transfer and/or appropriate from available funds, the sum of $42,322,565 to defray the necessary expenses of the departments, offices and boards of the Town, exclusive of the Regional Schools' budgets, or take any other action relative thereto.

plainEnglish.summary: This article funds every town department — police, fire, public works, health, library, and general government — for the fiscal year that began July 1, 2026, excluding the regional school assessment voted separately.
keyTakeaways: The town-side operating budget came to $42,322,565, growing about 3.05% inside the Select Board's 3.25% growth cap
The 2024 override reset the tax-levy baseline, which is why services could be funded without a new override this year
Total municipal spending including capital and enterprise subsidies was about $43.85 million
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote funded day-to-day town operations at the level the Finance Committee recommended.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have sent the board back for cuts or a revised budget late in the fiscal year.

financialImpact.explanation: Raised through property tax inside the levy limit, plus available funds — this article drives the bulk of the town's share of the annual property tax bill.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Authorize Borrowing for Town Hall HVAC and Emergency Power Replacement Project
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or borrow money by the issuance of bonds or notes a sum of money to be expended by the Town Manager for the Town Hall HVAC replacement and emergency power replacement, including all costs incidental and related thereto; or take any other action relative thereto.

plainEnglish.summary: This article authorized $2.75 million in borrowing to replace the aging Town Hall heating, cooling, and emergency power systems — as an all-electric heat-pump project.
keyTakeaways: The full project is worth $3.75 million, but a $1 million Commonwealth construction grant cuts what Town borrows
The replacement is all-electric heat pumps, consistent with the town's climate goals
This replaced a controversial 2025 borrowing package that had bundled too many projects
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote authorized bonds so the work could proceed with the state grant secured.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have left the 1970s-era building systems in place and risked losing the grant.

financialImpact.explanation: Borrowing authorization; the remainder of the $3,750,000 project is covered by a $1,000,000 Commonwealth grant.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Regional School District Assessment
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will raise and appropriate, transfer and/or appropriate from available funds, the sum of $82,830,682 to defray the necessary expenses of the Regional School District, or take any other action relative thereto.

plainEnglish.summary: This article paid the town's share of the regional school district's budget — by far the largest single line on any Town warrant, covering the high school, R.J. Grey Junior High, and the elementary schools the town shares with Boxborough.
keyTakeaways: the town's FY2027 assessment is $82,830,682 — roughly two-thirds of everything the town votes on in a typical year
The assessment is calculated under the regional district agreement, weighted by enrollment and property values, so Town Meeting cannot freely cut it
An effort to reject the assessment earlier in 2026 failed to gain traction; the article passed comfortably
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote funded the regional schools for the year, as the district agreement obligates both towns.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have refused the assessment — but state law and the regional agreement would still require the towns to fund the district.

financialImpact.explanation: The single largest appropriation Town votes on each year; the A-B district's total FY27 budget is substantially larger, with Boxborough covering a smaller share.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Appropriate Community Preservation Funds
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will appropriate or set aside for later appropriation, and authorize and direct the Select Board and the Town Manager to expend or set aside the following amounts listed below for community preservation purposes, with such expenditures to be subject to conditions listed in the Article's Summary and to be further specified in award letters from the Community Preservation Committee, with each item considered a separate appropriation:

plainEnglish.summary: The annual Community Preservation Act package: 14 separate appropriations totaling about $2.28 million, funded entirely by the CPA property-tax surcharge and its state match — not the general levy.
keyTakeaways: Biggest line: $598,500 to restore the Town Hall clock tower
Also funds the Apple Tree arboretum trail, Theatre III, McManus Manor affordable housing, and an $850,940 open-space set-aside
Includes scheduled debt payments on past CPA purchases, including Wetherbee Woods from 2024
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote approved all 14 CPA projects and set-asides as one package, exactly as the Community Preservation Committee ranked them.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have deferred all fourteen projects for a year, since the article was voted as a single package.

financialImpact.explanation: Drawn from the CPA General Fund ($1,959,196), the Historic Set-Aside ($40,800), and Open Space Set-Aside ($279,400) — money raised by the CPA surcharge with annual state matching revenue.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, voted on day two of the 2026 meeting.

articles.title: Authorize Acquisition of Property Located at 46 Taylor Road
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote to: 1. authorize the Select Board to acquire by purchase, gift, eminent domain or otherwise, and accept the deed of a fee simple interest, for open space, passive recreation and conservation purposes under M.G.L. Chapter 44B, Section 8C, the Community Preservation Act, that certain parcel of land containing approximately 5.80 acres, more or less, known as 46 Taylor Road in Town… 2. appropriate $1,445,000 for the purchase of 46 Taylor Road as described above… or take any other action relative thereto.

plainEnglish.summary: This article bought 5.8 acres at 46 Taylor Road for permanent open space and conservation — continuing the town's long pattern of land-banking with CPA funds.
keyTakeaways: The purchase price is $1.4 million plus $45,000 for due diligence: $1 million from the CPA open-space set-aside and up to $445,000 in bonding
The Town Conservation Trust later donated $116,620 from a record fundraising campaign to reduce the town's cost
The land becomes town-owned conservation land, not merely restricted private property
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote protected the parcel from development as town-owned open space forever.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have left the parcel available for private development.

financialImpact.explanation: $1,400,000 purchase price plus $45,000 due diligence; $1,000,000 from the CPA Open Space Set-Aside, up to $445,000 bonded for 20 years or less.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Approve Tax Increment Financing for Insulet Corporation — 35 Nagog Park
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote, pursuant to M.G.L. c.40, § 59 and M.G.L. c.23A, §§ 3A-3F to authorize the Select Board to (a) approve and execute a Tax Increment Financing ("TIF") Agreement between the Town and Insulet Corporation, Inc. for the property shown on Assessors Map B4-3-1, containing approximately 6.54 acres located at 35 Nagog Park, Town, MA, on terms and conditions deemed by the Select Board to be in the best interest of the Town; and (b) authorize the Select Board to execute any necessary documents relating thereto, and to take such other actions as may be necessary or appropriate to obtain approval of and implement the TIF Agreement and Certified Project application; or to take any other action in relation thereto.

plainEnglish.summary: The most-discussed article of the 2026 meeting: a tax-increment-financing deal giving Insulet — the insulin-pump maker at Nagog Park — a stepped-down property-tax exemption on its expansion in exchange for keeping and growing jobs in Town.
keyTakeaways: A TIF does not cut taxes outright; the company pays slowly rising taxes on the new value while the town gains investment it otherwise might not
Insulet is one of the town's largest employers and property taxpayers, which is why the debate ran long
The Select Board signed off on terms it judged in the town's interest before bringing the deal to the floor
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote authorized the TIF agreement, locking in the negotiated tax schedule for the project.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have cancelled the negotiated deal and left the expansion on the ordinary tax rolls.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Amend Zoning Bylaw and Map to Establish Nagog Park Innovation Overlay District
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote to amend the Zoning Bylaw and Zoning Map as follows and to renumber or alphabetize as necessary to accommodate such changes; or take any other action relative thereto:

plainEnglish.summary: Created a new Innovation Overlay District over the Nagog Park office park, giving the town modern flexible zoning tools to keep commercial property productive as office demand shifts.
keyTakeaways: Overlay districts add options on top of the base zoning; nothing underneath is removed
The district covers the 35 Nagog Park area where Insulet expanded — zoning and the TIF article worked as a pair
Two-thirds of town meeting members had to approve, since zoning changes require a supermajority
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote added the overlay, expanding what landowners can build there with town review.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote would have kept the office park under its existing, more restrictive zoning.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Amend Zoning Bylaw Related to Residential Additions on Nonconforming Lots
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote to amend the Zoning Bylaw by deleting the current Section 8.1.4 and replacing it with the following: 8.1.4 Extensions, alterations or changes of Single- and Two-Family Dwellings on Nonconforming Lots – One or more extensions, alterations or changes to a single or two-family residential STRUCTURE on a nonconforming LOT shall be deemed not to increase any nonconformity and shall not require special permits under Section 8.1.5, provided that such extensions, alterations or changes comply with all applicable dimensional requirements…

plainEnglish.summary: A quiet but important fix: homeowners on older, smaller-than-required lots can renovate or add on without a special permit hearing, as long as the work meets today's dimensional rules.
keyTakeaways: Roughly a quarter of the town's houses sit on lots that predate the current zoning sizes and are technically 'nonconforming'
Before, even a compliant porch or addition could trigger a months-long special-permit process
Housing-latency articles like this and the 2025 ADU reform aim to remove friction without changing neighborhood character
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote let compliant renovations on legacy lots proceed by right.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: A no vote kept the special-permit requirement for additions on nonconforming lots.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results, the town, May 2026 electronic vote.

articles.title: Amend Zoning Bylaw to Increase Affordability Requirements in the MBTA Overlay District
articles.originalText: To see if the Town will vote to amend the Zoning Bylaw by deleting the current Section 4.4.6 and …(full replacement text as set out in the 2026 warrant, increasing affordability requirements for housing in the MBTA Communities Overlay District)

plainEnglish.summary: The one article of the 2026 meeting that went nowhere: a proposal to raise affordable-housing requirements inside the MBTA Communities overlay the town adopted in 2024. The Select Board moved to take no action, and town meeting agreed.
keyTakeaways: "Take no action" is how town meeting skips an article without killing the topic forever — it can return on a future warrant
Supporters wanted more affordable units per development; opponents worried the requirement would stall the multifamily housing the 2024 overlay just unlocked
The no-action motion itself was voted by counted ballot: 220–48
plainEnglish.votingYesMeans: A yes vote on the article would have imposed higher affordability set-asides in the overlay district.
plainEnglish.votingNoMeans: The town ultimately took no action, leaving the 2024 affordability rules exactly as adopted.

officialOutcome.sourceNote: Official Town Meeting results list Article 20 as "No Action Taken" — town website, May 2026.

historicalVotes.title: Accessory Dwelling Unit bylaw amendment (Article 30)
historicalVotes.summary: To comply with the state Affordable Homes Act, Town removed owner-occupancy requirements, design criteria, and parking mandates for ADUs within half a mile of the South Town rail station, and grandfathered existing nonconforming ADUs.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The ADU reform opened the door for the housing-flexibility articles that followed — like the 2026 renovation fix for nonconforming lots.

historicalVotes.title: FY2025 operating levy limit override — $6.6 million
historicalVotes.summary: Facing health-insurance and inflation costs, the town asked voters to permanently raise the tax limit by $6.6 million for schools and municipal government. It passed by just 37 votes out of more than 6,300 cast.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The override reset the levy baseline for every budget article since — the reason FY27 municipal spending could grow a modest 3.05% without a new override.

historicalVotes.title: MBTA Communities Overlay District (Article 12)
historicalVotes.summary: Town Meeting ended the town's 75-year single-family-only zoning history by allowing multifamily housing by right near the South Town commuter-rail station, with 10 deed-restricted affordable units required per 100, in perpetuity.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Every MBTA-overlay zoning debate at the 2026 meeting — including the affordability question town meeting declined to act on — builds on this decision.

historicalVotes.title: Wetherbee Woods conservation purchase (Article 1)
historicalVotes.summary: Town bought 33.11 wooded acres at 19 & 35 Wetherbee Street — described as the "Agricultural Gateway to the Town" — for $3.68 million using a state grant, CPA funds, CPA-backed borrowing, and a $100,000 gift from the Town Conservation Trust.
historicalVotes.tally: Passed by 2/3 voice vote (364 voters present)
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: The 46 Taylor Road purchase and the CPA package reuse this exact funding recipe: state money first, CPA second, private fundraising third, bonding last.

historicalVotes.title: $5.42M PFAS filtration at the Central Town Water Treatment Plant
historicalVotes.summary: Water District voters funded granular-activated-carbon PFAS treatment at the Central Town plant, with the South Town plant's larger retrofit approved by regulators to operate in May 2024.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: the town's water is funded and voted separately from town meeting — a useful reminder that some key local spending decisions happen outside Town Meeting entirely.

historicalVotes.title: Debt exclusion for the new Gates Elementary School
historicalVotes.summary: Voters approved excluding the bond costs of the town's share of the new Douglas–Gates elementary campus from Prop 2½ limits — one of two exclusions on that ballot, the other being the fire station.
historicalVotes.tally: 1,122 – 364 (fire station exclusion passed 1,169–315 the same day)
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Pay-for-the-study, got-the-state-grant: the same playbook behind the $36.7M MSBA award and behind the 2026 Town Hall HVAC borrowing that leans on a $1M state grant.

historicalVotes.title: Debt exclusion for A-B Regional High School addition and remodel
historicalVotes.summary: A generation ago, town voters approved the town's share of a major expansion and remodel of the regional high school by a wide margin on an exclusion ballot.
historicalVotes.relevanceNote: Two decades of school-facility investment ends up where the money is actually voted every year: the annual Article 8 regional school assessment.

demoSession.headline: Article 4 called to the floor
demoSession.caption: The FY2027 municipal operating budget — $42,322,565 — comes up under the Select Board's 3.25% growth cap. Floor opens for questions.

demoSession.headline: Budget debate
demoSession.caption: Finance Committee presents; town meeting members press on levy growth and where the $6.6M override is absorbed.

demoSession.headline: The school assessment
demoSession.caption: Article 8 asks for $82,830,682 — the largest single line on any Town warrant, the town's share of the regional schools.

demoSession.headline: Land for conservation
demoSession.caption: Article 13: 5.8 acres at 46 Taylor Road for $1,445,000, backed by a record Town Conservation Trust campaign.

demoSession.headline: The Insulet TIF debate
demoSession.caption: Longest debate of the meeting: a tax-increment-financing deal for the insulin-pump maker at 35 Nagog Park, approved 242–18.

demoSession.headline: Article 20 goes a different way
demoSession.caption: The Select Board moves to take no action on the MBTA overlay affordability amendment — the only article that died this year (220–48).

demoSession.headline: The CPA package closes the meeting
demoSession.caption: Day two: Article 10 bundles 14 community-preservation appropriations — clock tower to open space — and passes 327–15.
